presentation.subject: ERC-20 Token Standard — Deep Dive & Practice

slides.title: Introduction — Why ERC-20 Matters
slides.quote: "Today we are starting one of the most important topics in Solidity development: token standards."
slides.transition: Now we use all those concepts together to understand something that almost every blockchain developer works with: ERC-20 tokens.

slides.title: What is a Standard? — The USB Analogy
slides.analogy: Think about USB. Different companies manufacture laptops, keyboards, and storage devices — but because they follow the USB standard, they all work together.
slides.erc20_point: ERC-20 works the same way. If a token follows the ERC-20 standard, any wallet, exchange, or application already knows how to interact with it.
slides.key_insight: MetaMask does not need custom code for every token. A DEX does not need different logic for every token. The standard handles it.

slides.title: What is ERC-20?
slides.definition: ERC-20 (Ethereum Request for Comments #20) is a standard that defines how fungible tokens should behave on the Ethereum blockchain.
slides.fungible_explanation: Fungible means every unit is interchangeable — identical in value and properties.

slides.title: Core ERC-20 Functions
slides.subtitle: Every ERC-20 token must implement these 6 functions

functions.name: totalSupply()
functions.description: How many tokens exist in total?

functions.name: balanceOf(address)
functions.description: How many tokens does this wallet hold?

functions.name: transfer(to, amount)
functions.description: Send your tokens directly to another wallet.

functions.name: approve(spender, amount)
functions.description: Give another address permission to spend your tokens.
functions.example: Alice approves DEX to spend80 MTK

functions.name: allowance(owner, spender)
functions.description: Check how many tokens a spender is allowed to use.

functions.name: transferFrom(from, to, amount)
functions.description: An approved spender transfers tokens on behalf of the owner.
functions.example: DEX moves 100 MTK from Alice to Bob

slides.note: approve, allowance, and transferFrom are extremely important in DeFi protocols.

slides.title: How Token Balances Are Stored

wrong_way.label: ❌  Wrong — Does NOT scale

right_way.label: ✅  Correct — Using a Mapping
right_way.code:
mapping(address => uint256) public balanceOf;

// Stores every wallet's balance in one structure

slides.insight: This is exactly why we learned mappings in earlier lectures. They are the perfect data structure for token balances.
slides.supply_var: uint256 public totalSupply;   // total tokens that exist

slides.title: Transfer Event
slides.label: event Transfer + emit
why_important: MetaMask uses Transfer events to show token activity
Etherscan tracks all token transfers via this event
DeFi frontends subscribe to this event to update UI

slides.title: The Approval System — Why It Exists
slides.problem: Decentralized applications (DEXes, lending protocols) often need to move tokens on behalf of users. But a contract cannot simply take your tokens without permission.
slides.analogy: Alice wants to swap 100 USDT on Uniswap. She must first APPROVE Uniswap to spend 100 USDT on her behalf. Then Uniswap can call transferFrom() to move those tokens.
slides.key_sentence: approve() does NOT transfer tokens. It only stores permission.

slides.title: Practical 2 — approve() & Approval Event
slides.label: approve() function + Approval event
key_points: No tokens move when approve() is called
Only permission is stored in the allowance mapping
spender = the address allowed to spend
The Approval event notifies the outside world

slides.title: transferFrom() — Delegated Transfer
slides.label: transferFrom() function
step_explanations: Check the owner (from) has enough tokens
Check the caller has enough allowance
Move tokens from owner to recipient

slides.title: OpenZeppelin ERC-20 — Production Ready
slides.message: Everything we just built manually was for learning. In production, never rewrite ERC-20 from scratch. Use audited, battle-tested implementations like OpenZeppelin.
why_openzeppelin: Audited by top security firms — widely trusted
Used in USDC, AAVE, Compound, Uniswap, and thousands more
Just inherit and call _mint() in the constructor
Same concepts: inheritance, events, mappings — all inside

concepts_connection.title: Everything from previous lectures is here:

slides.title: Understanding decimals()
slides.explanation: Most ERC-20 tokens use 18 decimal places. Solidity only works with integers — decimals are a display convention.
slides.analogy: Just like 1 ETH = 1,000,000,000,000,000,000 wei — the display shows 1 ETH but internally it is always an integer.
slides.note: Token decimals are only a display convention. All Solidity arithmetic operates on raw integers.

items.detail: Standard interface for fungible tokens on Ethereum
Every unit is identical and interchangeable in value
Total number of tokens that exist in the contract
Owner sends tokens directly to another address
Owner grants a spender permission to spend tokens
Query how many tokens a spender is permitted to use
Approved spender moves tokens on behalf of the owner
Emitted on every token movement — wallets track this

slides.title: Thank You
slides.subtitle: Lecture 8 Complete
slides.key_message: Today we moved from learning Solidity features individually to understanding an actual blockchain standard that powers billions of dollars in value.
recap: ERC-20 is a standard — not just one contract
Transfer & Approval events power wallets and explorers
decimals() is a display convention — integers internally
slides.closing_statement: From this point onward, you should be able to look at any ERC-20 contract and understand exactly why mappings, events, inheritance, interfaces, and modifiers are being used. You now speak the language of token development.
